summary: Rupatadine is a second-generation, long-acting antihistamine that combines selective peripheral H1-receptor antagonism with platelet-activating factor (PAF) antagonism. It is used once daily to treat allergic rhinitis and chronic urticaria with little sedation. It is metabolized by CYP3A4, so strong inhibitors (e.g., ketoconazole, erythromycin) and grapefruit juice can raise levels, and concomitant alcohol or QT-prolonging drugs should be avoided.
indications: Symptomatic treatment of allergic rhinitis (seasonal and perennial)
Symptomatic treatment of chronic spontaneous urticaria

dosage.n: Per regional SmPC; weight-based pediatric dosing

admin: Take one 10 mg tablet once daily
May be taken with or without food
Avoid grapefruit juice, which can raise rupatadine levels
Use the measuring device provided for the oral solution in children
moa: Rupatadine is a dual antagonist that selectively blocks peripheral histamine H1 receptors and platelet-activating factor (PAF) receptors. H1 antagonism prevents histamine-mediated allergic symptoms (rhinorrhea, sneezing, itch), while PAF antagonism adds anti-inflammatory activity relevant to allergic inflammation. Its low CNS penetration accounts for minimal sedation.

absolute: Hypersensitivity to rupatadine or any excipient
relative: Known QT prolongation or significant electrolyte disturbance
Moderate to severe hepatic or renal impairment (not studied)
monitor: ECG/QT when combined with QT-prolonging drugs

preg: There are limited data on the use of rupatadine in pregnant women; as a precaution it is preferable to avoid its use during pregnancy unless clearly necessary.
lact: Rupatadine is excreted in the milk of animals; excretion in human milk is unknown, so use during breastfeeding is not recommended.
renal: Rupatadine has not been studied in patients with renal impairment; use with caution as no dosing recommendation is established.
hepatic: Rupatadine has not been studied in patients with hepatic impairment; its use is not recommended in moderate to severe hepatic impairment.

major: Strong CYP3A4 inhibitors (ketoconazole, itraconazole, erythromycin, clarithromycin) - markedly increase rupatadine exposure; avoid co-administration
Drugs that prolong the QT interval - additive risk of QT prolongation; avoid combination
moderate: Statins metabolized by CYP3A4 (theoretical exposure changes)
interactions.food: Grapefruit juice increases rupatadine exposure and should be avoided; other food has no clinically important effect
interactions.alcohol: Co-administration with alcohol may potentiate alcohol effects; avoid
interactions.diagnostics: May suppress skin-prick allergy test reactivity - withhold for several days before testing

rare: QT prolongation (theoretical, especially with interacting drugs)

monitoring: Somnolence, particularly when starting or with other sedatives
ECG/QT if used with other QT-prolonging agents
counsel: Take once daily; it usually causes little or no drowsiness, but take care until you know how it affects you
Avoid grapefruit juice and limit alcohol while taking it
Tell your doctor about heart rhythm problems or other medicines, especially antifungals and certain antibiotics
Stop antihistamines a few days before any allergy skin tests
Not recommended in pregnancy or breastfeeding unless your doctor advises
pk: Antihistaminic effect within ~1 hour of dosing
Peak plasma concentration about 0.75-1 hour after oral dosing
Approximately 6 hours (active metabolites contribute to longer effect)
Store below 30 C; protect from moisture
pearls: Not FDA-approved in the United States; authorized in the EU/EMA and many countries (BNF/SmPC source) - dosing reflects the SmPC
Dual H1 plus PAF antagonism may add anti-inflammatory benefit over pure H1 blockers
CYP3A4 substrate - avoid strong inhibitors, grapefruit juice, and QT-prolonging combinations
Largely non-sedating, but some somnolence can occur
missed: Take the missed dose as soon as you remember on the same day. If it is almost time for the next dose, skip it and take the next dose as scheduled - do not double up.
overdose: Single doses well above the therapeutic dose were generally well tolerated, with somnolence as the most likely effect. There is no specific antidote; management is supportive with symptomatic care and cardiac monitoring (including ECG) if a large overdose or QT-prolonging co-medication is involved.
